Ticks are blood-sucking arthropods that transmit a variety of disease-causing pathogens. These pathogens are typically sustained in enzootic cycles involving multiple host species and transmitted to humans through infected tick bites. *Ehrlichia chaffeensis* and *Anaplasma phagocytophilum* are common tick-borne pathogens in the southern United States, each associated with a different tick vector and distinctive set of host species. Their geographic ranges are associated with multiple climate and land cover variables ([Yabsley et al. 2005](#tick-refs)). However, the most important environmental predictors vary geographically, reflecting distinctive ecological conditions in different parts of the species’ ranges ([Wimberly et al. 2008b](#tick-refs)). Climate is the main determinant of pathogen presence in the eastern U.S., whereas forest cover and fragmentation constrain the western range boundaries. In the Mississippi Alluvial Valley, there are strong effects of forest cover and flooding ([Manangan et al. 2007](#tick-refs)). Bayesian hierarchical models that include environmental predictors with spatially varying coefficients and conditional autoregressive terms can accurately predict the regional distributions of both pathgens ([Wimberly et al. 2008a](#tick-refs)). This work showed that it is possible to model the geographic distributions of tick-borne pathogens in sentinel hosts and emphasize the importance of accounting for spatially heterogeneity and spatial autocorrelation to account for their complex environmental relationships.
